classContent: Students introduced themselves and explored self-awareness, logic and personal viewpoints.
The class used the glacier-collapse and mudslide topic to develop an original perspective.
Students were asked to turn an impromptu response into a structured speech with clearer logic, transitions and supporting detail.

homework.title: Your perspective on the glacier event
steps: Turn your impromptu response about the glacier collapse and mudslides into a roughly 200–400-word speech.
Develop your own perspective, with clearer structure, logic and supporting detail.
Use transitions such as first, second and finally.
homework.prepareFor: Be ready to present at the beginning of the next class.
homework.note: The five-minute curriculum target is not the length assigned for this lesson.

classContent: The class practised impromptu answers with a reason, an example and a useful audience message, applying feedback between attempts.
Students reviewed more than ten recent-news articles and used cause, effect, impact and solution to summarise an event and develop a viewpoint.
Group presentations introduced the structure of Original Oratory while highlighting the need to strengthen basic delivery skills.
The final topic was AI surveillance and the distribution of power.

homework.title: AI surveillance and the distribution of power
steps: Write a speech of roughly 300–500 words about AI surveillance and the distribution of power.
Organise the speech around cause, effect, impact and solution.
Practise delivering the ideas without reading directly from a full script; use note cards for guidance if needed.
homework.prepareFor: Be ready to deliver the speech at the next class.

classContent: Students explored fear of the stage and fear of content.
The class practised awareness of eyes, feet, hands, face and emotion, along with articulation and emotional delivery.
A world-champion example, impromptu structures and specific details supported repeated speaking attempts.
Feedback was applied through repeat responses.

homework.title: A self-introduction with specific details
steps: Introduce your name and one thing about yourself.
Develop three supporting parts: when you started, what you learned, and what you want to do in the future.
Include specific details so the audience learns more about you.
Say the speech aloud two or three times.
homework.prepareFor: Prepare to present in the next class.
homework.note: Writing is the first step; rehearsal is part of the homework.

classContent: This class was cancelled.
Voice, body and articulation warm-ups led into self-introductions and impromptu structure.
Students considered finding RMB 10,000 in a wallet as an impromptu prompt.
The Nepal–China glacier-flooding topic was used to practise an organised speech.
Coaching included numbered points, voice and audience-appropriate language.

homework.title: Self-introduction or glacier speech
steps: Practise your self-introduction speech, the printed glacier speech, or both.
For the glacier speech, practise explaining the importance of being careful as the world and climate change.
homework.prepareFor: Prepare to deliver your selected speech at the next class.
homework.note: Homework recorded in the teacher’s September 7 follow-up to this class.

classContent: The class reviewed the self-introduction and glacier-speech homework through speaking attempts.
Self-introductions focused on one thing about the speaker, supported by when it began, what they learned, and future plans.
Students tried presenting without relying on a full script, and later attempts were included in the feedback.
Students repeatedly practised self-introductions around one central personal idea.
They developed when the idea began, what they learned, future plans and a return to the main idea at the end.
Coaching covered breath, voice, specific details, posture, grammar and managing time.
Voice and body warm-ups led into self-introduction and impromptu structure.
Students practised answering a superpower prompt with structured speaking support.
The focus was developing students' own ideas and building readiness to present.

homework.title: Write your own self-introduction
steps: Write a self-introduction in your own words, using your own ideas.
Rehearse it so you can speak with less reliance on the paper.
Try to memorise it if possible; use script support where needed.
homework.prepareFor: Present your self-introduction at the next class.
homework.note: The goal is a student-written speech.

classContent: Voice, articulation and body warm-ups led into unguided introductions.
Returning students added a clap or hooray challenge.
Students explored occupations and applied feedback in second or third rounds.
A shared story practised happy, scrunched, sad and shocked facial expressions, along with stronger projection.

homework.title: Your chosen occupation speech
steps: Practise and memorise your chosen occupation speech.
Record a video if possible as a record of your practice.
homework.prepareFor: Be ready to present at the next class.
homework.note: A video is preferred, rather than required.

classContent: The class practised voice, articulation, hand control and pace during speaking turns.
Students also worked on attentive listening while classmates were speaking.
Students discussed whether people should keep doing something they are not good at.
They practised taking a position and organising reasons with first, second and finally.
Coaching focused on clear explanations, audience direction, audible articulation and respectful listening.
